title: Kepler Conjecture: Sphere Packing
description: The face-centered cubic lattice achieves the maximum sphere packing density of π/(3√2). Part of Hilbert's 18th Problem, proven by Hales (1998) and formally verified by Flyspeck (2014).

overview.historicalContext:
In 1611, Johannes Kepler conjectured that the face-centered cubic arrangement — the way grocers stack oranges — achieves the maximum possible density for packing congruent spheres in three-dimensional space. This seemingly simple question resisted proof for nearly 400 years.

Carl Friedrich Gauss (1831) proved the weaker result that FCC is optimal among lattice packings, where sphere centers form a regular lattice. Axel Thue (1892) solved the two-dimensional analogue, showing that hexagonal packing is optimal for disks in the plane, with a rigorous proof later completed by László Fejes Tóth (1940).

The full Kepler Conjecture was finally proven by Thomas Hales in 1998, using a computer-assisted approach. The proof, spanning 250+ pages of mathematics and 40,000+ lines of computer code, reduced the problem to verifying approximately 5000 linear programming problems via a Delaunay star decomposition. After a four-year review by 12 referees, the proof was published in the Annals of Mathematics in 2005, though the referees noted they were '99% certain' of correctness — prompting Hales to pursue formal verification.

The Flyspeck project (2014) formally verified Hales' proof in HOL Light, making it the first major computer-assisted proof to receive full formal verification. In 2016, Maryna Viazovska solved the sphere packing problem in dimension 8 (E₈ lattice) and, with collaborators, dimension 24 (Leech lattice), using a groundbreaking technique based on modular forms. She received the 2022 Fields Medal for this work.
overview.problemStatement: **Theorem (Kepler-Hales):** The maximum density for sphere packing in ℝ³ is π/(3√2) ≈ 74.05%, achieved by the face-centered cubic lattice.
overview.text: The face-centered cubic lattice achieves the maximum sphere packing density of π/(3√2). Part of Hilbert's 18th Problem, proven by Hales (1998) and formally verified by Flyspeck (2014).
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization is structured in seven parts. Part 1 defines sphere volume, disk area, and the PackingDensity structure (density in [0,1]). Part 2 covers 2D packing: the hexagonal density π/(2√3) with positivity proof, kissing number 6, and Thue's optimality theorem (axiomatized). Part 3 defines the FCC density π/(3√2) with positivity proof, alternative representation π√2/6, kissing number 12, and numerical bounds (0.74, 0.75). Part 4 axiomatizes the Kepler conjecture and Gauss's lattice theorem. Part 5 introduces higher dimensions: E₈ density π⁴/384 and Viazovska's theorem. Part 6 documents applications. Part 7 proves the density comparison chain 2D > 3D > 8D via axiomatized numerical inequalities.
keyInsights: The PackingDensity structure (0 ≤ δ ≤ 1) provides a clean type-theoretic abstraction that unifies packing density comparisons across dimensions
The Kepler Conjecture is the first major theorem whose proof was formally verified after computer-assisted discovery — pioneering a new paradigm in mathematical proof
FCC and HCP achieve the same density π/(3√2) despite different stacking patterns (ABCABC vs ABAB), reflecting the non-uniqueness of optimal packings
Viazovska's dimension 8 proof introduced a revolutionary technique — constructing optimal auxiliary functions from modular forms — that has no analogue in dimension 3
The density comparison 2D > 3D > 8D reflects the curse of dimensionality: the ratio of sphere volume to ambient space decreases rapidly with dimension
The 400-year gap between conjecture (1611) and proof (1998) illustrates how geometric intuition can be correct long before rigorous verification is possible

sections.title: Module Docstring
sections.summary: Historical introduction covering Kepler (1611), Gauss (1831), Thue (1892), Hales (1998), Flyspeck (2014), and Viazovska (2016). Lists formalization status and references.
sections.mathContext: Introduces the sphere packing problem: maximize the packing density $\delta = \lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{\text{Vol}(\bigcup B_i \cap B(0,R))}{\text{Vol}(B(0,R))}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The conjectured optimum is $\delta_{\text{FCC}} = \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.7405$.

sections.title: Part 1: Basic Definitions
sections.summary: Defines sphereVolume (4/3)πr³, diskArea πr², and PackingDensity structure with 0 ≤ density ≤ 1 invariants.
sections.mathContext: Defines $V_{\text{sphere}}(r) = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, $A_{\text{disk}}(r) = \pi r^2$, and the $\texttt{PackingDensity}$ structure with field $\delta \in [0, 1]$ satisfying $0 \leq \delta$ and $\delta \leq 1$.

sections.title: Part 2: Hexagonal Packing (2D)
sections.summary: Defines hexagonalDensity2D = π/(2√3), proves positivity, axiomatizes < 1, defines kissingNumber2D = 6, and axiomatizes Thue's optimality theorem via Voronoi cell argument.
sections.mathContext: Defines $\delta_{\text{hex}} = \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.9069$, proves $\delta_{\text{hex}} > 0$, axiomatizes $\delta_{\text{hex}} < 1$. Sets kissing number $\tau_2 = 6$. Axiomatizes Thue's theorem: $\forall\, \delta,\; \delta \leq \delta_{\text{hex}}$ (hexagonal packing is optimal in $\mathbb{R}^2$).

sections.title: Part 3: FCC Lattice (3D)
sections.summary: Defines fccDensity = π/(3√2) with positivity proof, alternative fccDensityAlt = π√2/6, kissingNumber3D = 12, and axiomatized numerical bounds 0.74 < δ < 0.75.
sections.mathContext: Defines $\delta_{\text{FCC}} = \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}}$ with alternative form $\frac{\pi\sqrt{2}}{6}$. Proves $\delta_{\text{FCC}} > 0$. Sets kissing number $\tau_3 = 12$. Axiomatizes bounds $0.74 < \delta_{\text{FCC}} < 0.75$.

sections.title: Part 4: The Kepler Conjecture
sections.summary: Axiomatizes kepler_conjecture (all packings ≤ fccDensity), proves fcc_is_optimal_3D, and axiomatizes gauss_lattice_theorem (lattice-only version).
sections.mathContext: Axiomatizes the Kepler conjecture: $\forall\, \delta \in \texttt{PackingDensity},\; \delta \leq \delta_{\text{FCC}}$. Proves $\delta_{\text{FCC}}$ is an optimal $\texttt{PackingDensity}$. Axiomatizes Gauss's lattice theorem: $\forall$ lattice packings $\Lambda$, $\delta(\Lambda) \leq \delta_{\text{FCC}}$.

sections.title: Part 5: Higher Dimensions
sections.summary: Defines e8Density = π⁴/384 with positivity proof, kissing numbers k(8) = 240, k(24) = 196560, and axiomatizes viazovska_theorem_8d.
sections.mathContext: Defines $\delta_{E_8} = \frac{\pi^4}{384} \approx 0.2537$ with positivity proof. Sets kissing numbers $\tau_8 = 240$ and $\tau_{24} = 196560$. Axiomatizes Viazovska's theorem: $\forall$ packings in $\mathbb{R}^8$, $\delta \leq \delta_{E_8}$.

sections.title: Part 6: Applications
sections.summary: Documents applications to error-correcting codes (E₈, Leech lattice), crystallography (FCC metals), digital communications (Shannon bounds), and computational geometry.
sections.mathContext: Discusses applications: the $E_8$ and Leech lattices yield optimal error-correcting codes with minimum distance $d_{\min}$; FCC structure explains close-packed metals (Cu, Al, Au); sphere packing bounds connect to Shannon channel capacity $C = W \log_2(1 + S/N)$.

sections.title: Part 7: Density Comparison
sections.summary: Axiomatizes hexagonal_gt_fcc and fcc_gt_e8, then proves density_decreases_with_dimension: δ₂D > δ₃D > δ₈D. Exports section verifies all major results.
sections.mathContext: Axiomatizes $\delta_{\text{hex}} > \delta_{\text{FCC}}$ and $\delta_{\text{FCC}} > \delta_{E_8}$, then proves the chain $\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{3}} > \frac{\pi}{3\sqrt{2}} > \frac{\pi^4}{384}$, i.e., optimal packing density decreases: $\delta_2 > \delta_3 > \delta_8$.

conclusion.summary: The Kepler Conjecture is proven: the FCC lattice achieves the maximum sphere packing density π/(3√2) ≈ 74.05% in ℝ³. The formalization covers the 2D hexagonal optimality (Thue), 3D FCC optimality (Hales/Flyspeck), and 8D E₈ optimality (Viazovska), establishing the density comparison chain across dimensions.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: Hales' proof pioneered the paradigm of formally verified computer-assisted mathematics.

The Flyspeck project demonstrated that even proofs too large for human verification can be machine-checked, inspiring similar formal verification efforts (e.g., Gonthier's proof of the Four Color Theorem in Coq). Sphere packing theory connects to error-correcting codes, crystallography, and signal processing, with the E₈ and Leech lattices being among the most important discrete structures in mathematics.
openQuestions: What is the optimal sphere packing density in dimensions 4, 5, 6, 7, and 9-23?
Is there a proof of the Kepler Conjecture that does not require computer assistance?
Can Viazovska's modular forms technique be extended to other dimensions, or are 8 and 24 fundamentally special?
What is the optimal packing density for non-spherical objects (ellipsoids, tetrahedra) in ℝ³?
